nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a nonempty finite set of points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ have dimension $d$. Then the graph of $P$ is $d$-connected: it has more than $d$ vertices, and it stays connected after deleting any set of fewer than $d$ vertices.
nodes.title: Balinski's theorem

nodes.summary: The bottom element of the face lattice of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is the empty face.
nodes.title: Bottom of the face lattice

nodes.summary: The top element of the face lattice of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is the polytope $P$ itself.
nodes.title: Top of the face lattice

nodes.summary: The dimension of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is the dimension of its affine hull, that is, of the linear subspace parallel to $\operatorname{aff} P = \operatorname{aff} s$. A $d$-polytope is a polytope of dimension $d$.
nodes.title: Dimension of a polytope

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set of points and $F$ a face of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$. Then In particular every face of a polytope is again a polytope, spanned by some of the given points.
nodes.title: A face of a polytope is the convex hull of the vertices it contains

nodes.summary: The set of vertices (extreme points) of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is finite for every finite set $s$, since it is contained in $s$.
nodes.title: The vertex set of a polytope is finite

nodes.summary: For a finite set $s$, the face lattice $L(P)$ of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is the set of all faces of $P$, including $\emptyset$ and $P$, ordered by inclusion. It is a finite complete lattice: the meet of a family of faces is their intersection (with $P$, for the empty family), and the join is the meet of all common upper bounds. Its bottom element is the empty face and its top element is $P$. The isomorphism…
nodes.title: Face lattice of a polytope

nodes.summary: For a finite set $s$ and $k \ge 0$, the face number $f_k(P)$ of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is the number of nonempty faces of $P$ whose affine hull has dimension $k$. Thus $f_0$ counts the vertices, $f_1$ the edges and, for a $d$-polytope, $f_{d-1}$ the facets, while $f_d = 1$ counts $P$ itself. The vector $(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{d-1})$ is the f-vector of $P$.
nodes.title: Face numbers of a polytope

nodes.summary: For every finite set $s$, the set of faces of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ is finite: each face is $\operatorname{conv} T$ for a subset $T \subseteq s$, so there are at most $2^{|s|}$ of them. This makes the face numbers, which are counts of faces, meaningful.
nodes.title: A polytope has finitely many faces

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set of points in a real normed space $E$ (for example $\mathbb{R}^n$) and let $P = \operatorname{conv} s$. A face of $P$ is either the empty set or a set of the form for a continuous linear functional $\ell$ on $E$: the points where $\ell$ attains its maximum over $P$. The zero functional gives $F = P$, so $P$ is a face of itself; the empty set is a face by convention. In Lean, `faces s` is the…
nodes.title: Faces of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: The graph of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ has the vertices (extreme points) of $P$ as its vertices, and two distinct vertices $u, v$ are adjacent when the segment $[u, v]$ is a face of $P$, that is, an edge. Every one-dimensional face of a polytope is such a segment between two vertices, so this is the 1-skeleton of $P$. By Steinitz's theorem, the graphs of 3-polytopes are exactly the 3-connected planar graphs.
nodes.title: The graph of a polytope

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be finite, $P = \operatorname{conv} s$, and let $A$ be any family of faces of $P$. Then $P \cap \bigcap_{F \in A} F$ is a face of $P$; for the empty family it is $P$ itself. Since there are only finitely many faces, this reduces to finite intersections, where the sum of the exposing functionals exposes the intersection.
nodes.title: Intersections of faces are faces

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set, $T \subseteq s$, and $\ell$ a continuous linear functional with $\ell(y) \le V$ for all $y \in s$, $\ell(y) = V$ for all $y \in T$, and $\ell(y) < V$ for $y \in s \setminus T$. Then $\operatorname{conv} T$ is a face of $\operatorname{conv} s$. (For $T = \emptyset$ the face is empty.) This is how faces of a polytope are produced from its vertex set alone: the face cut out by $\ell$ is the…
nodes.title: Faces cut out by a functional

nodes.summary: The polytope $P = \operatorname{conv} s$ of dimension $d$ is simplicial if every facet of $P$ (a nonempty face of dimension $d - 1$) contains exactly $d$ vertices of $P$, that is, is a $(d-1)$-simplex. Cyclic polytopes, and the convex hull of finitely many points in general position, are simplicial; their boundary complexes are simplicial spheres.
nodes.title: Simplicial polytope

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be finite, $F$ a face of $P = \operatorname{conv} s$, and $G$ a face of $F$ (an exposed subset of $F$). Then $G$ is a face of $P$. Together with the converse (a face of $P$ contained in $F$ is a face of $F$, Mathlib's `IsExposed.mono`), the faces of $F$ are exactly the faces of $P$ contained in $F$, so the face lattice of $F$ is the interval $[\emptyset, F]$ of the face lattice of $P$; that lattice…
nodes.title: A face of a face of a polytope is a face of the polytope

nodes.summary: A finite simple graph $G$ is the graph of a 3-dimensional convex polytope if and only if $G$ is planar and 3-connected.
nodes.title: Steinitz's theorem

fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.
